uncited: **Inputs:** A reference point cloud and a distorted point cloud, each consisting of a list of points with 3D spatial coordinates $(x, y, z)$ and color values.
**Outputs:** Six pairs of 2D images (reference and distorted) corresponding to the faces of a bounding cube, and a set of objective quality scores derived from 2D metrics applied to these pairs.
*   `x`, `y`, `z`: Floating-point spatial coordinates.
*   `r`, `g`, `b`: Color components (format depends on the specific 2D metric implementation, e.g., uint8 or float).
*   **Voxel Grid:** A 3D array or hash map mapping integer coordinates $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ to color values.
The grid dimensions are determined by the scaling factor $s$ and the target resolution of 1024x1024 for the projected images.
*   **Projection Images:** 2D arrays of size $1024 \times 1024$ (or defined by the scaling logic) storing the final pixel colors.
Iterate through all points in the point cloud.
Record the maximum ($w_{max}$) and minimum ($w_{min}$) coordinate values for each dimension ($x, y, z$).
Calculate the scaling factor $s$ to fit the model in a cubic volume of side 1024.
Apply a rigid rotation to the spatial coordinates using a rotation matrix $R$ calculated from the user-defined yaw and pitch angles.
If user interaction includes panning, add shift values $pan_x$ and $pan_y$ to the $x$ and $y$ coordinates respectively.
Quantize the final spatial coordinates to integer values $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$.
Define a bounding cube around the object.
Project the voxelized point cloud orthographically onto the 6 faces of the cube.
Apply 2D image metrics to each pair of projected reference and distorted images.
*   Compute one score for each of the 6 pairs of images.
Renders a voxelized point cloud to a 2D image by quantizing 3D coordinates, applying user-controlled panning, sorting by depth, and resolving overlaps.
This is the parent method that provides the interactive rendering framework. [Link](18548-point-cloud-projection-with-depth-sorting.md)
Methods such as PSNR, SSIM, and VIFP used to evaluate the projected images.
These are not voxelization methods but are the downstream consumers of the output of Orthographic Voxelization and Projection.
*   **Time Complexity:** Linear with respect to the number of points $N$ for the voxelization and projection steps ($O(N)$), as each point is processed once.
The metric computation is $O(P)$ where $P$ is the number of pixels (1024x1024x6).
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(N)$ to store the point clouds and $O(P)$ to store the 6 projection images.
*   Leverages well-established 2D image quality metrics.
*   Only provides 6 viewing angles, which may not capture all aspects of the 3D structure.
*   Relies on the assumption that 2D metrics correlate well with 3D perceptual quality, which may not always hold for complex geometries.
*   Requires the point cloud to be voxelized, which may introduce quantization artifacts.
*   **When to use:** When objective quality assessment of point clouds is required, and the computational cost of 3D-specific metrics is prohibitive or less validated.
*   **When not to use:** When a full 360-degree view is necessary, or when the point cloud has complex occlusions that are not well-represented by 6 orthogonal views.
The authors developed a rendering software that performs real-time voxelization and projection, allowing user interaction.
